'That's four notebooks of ideas, Leena,' Vikas said, tapping the table. 'When does the newsletter launch?'

Leena laughed weakly. 'When I finish planning it.'

'Which part is the hard one?'

'All of it.' She turned pages, then stopped with the pen in her hand. 'No, that's not true. Nearly all of this is fine. The only thing blocking me is the sign-up form, and I've drawn it three times.'

'So?'

'So...' She circled it in red. 'Tomorrow, nine-thirty, build the form. Just the form.' She wrote 9:30 beside the circle.

'And the other pages?'

'They can wait.' She closed the notebook. 'At nine-thirty I open the laptop, not the notebook.'

passage:
I'm Nandini, and for most of last year I was a champion planner and a terrible starter. I wanted to open a small reading room for children in our lane. I had pages and pages of ideas.
One evening my friend Hansa came over and said, "Show me the plan." I spread everything out on the floor. Hansa looked for a while and then said, "What can you do tomorrow?"
I didn't know. So I went through every page slowly, with a red pen. Most things needed other things first. But one didn't: ask Mrs D'Souza downstairs if her unused garage could be the room.
I circled it. Beside it I wrote: "Tomorrow, 6 p.m., after she's back from church."
The next evening I knocked. She said yes. That one circle turned a year of notes into an actual room.

qa.q: What did Nandini write beside the circled step?
qa.a: "Tomorrow, 6 p.m., after she's back from church."

qa.q: How might Nandini have felt when Hansa asked what could be done tomorrow?
qa.a: Nandini probably felt caught out and a little embarrassed, not knowing despite pages of plans.

qa.q: What else could Nandini do after the garage was agreed?
qa.a: Nandini could go back to the pages and circle the next single step with a time beside it, so the work keeps moving.

qa.q: How might Mrs D'Souza see Nandini's visit?
qa.a: Mrs D'Souza may be pleased to help, seeing the unused garage turned into something good for children in the lane.

grounding: It shows a young planner reviewing the pages, circling the one step that can be done tomorrow and putting a time beside it so the notes become work.

Mentor's note, fellowship check-in, 9 January
Noor has been planning her community health-literacy workshops since August. Her folder is thick: maps of the ward, lists of partners, draft posters, three possible timetables. At our last two check-ins, nothing had actually started. She seemed tired and a bit embarrassed about it.
Today I asked her to look through the whole folder and find one thing she could do tomorrow without waiting for anything else.
She turned pages for several minutes. Then she stopped at a list of partners, took my red pen and circled one line: "Ask the anganwadi worker in Ward 7 for a room." She wrote beside it: "Thursday, 10 a.m."
She looked lighter when she left. I will ask on Friday how the conversation went.
— Vishal

qa.q: What did Noor write beside the circled line?
How did Noor seem to feel at the earlier check-ins?
qa.a: She seemed tired and a bit embarrassed that nothing had started despite the thick folder.

qa.q: What else could Noor do after Thursday's visit?
qa.a: She could circle the next single step in the folder and give it a time, so planning keeps turning into action.

qa.q: How might Vishal see the change in Noor today?
qa.a: Vishal notices she looked lighter when she left and plans to check on Friday how the talk went.

grounding: It shows a young woman looking over her plans, circling the one step she can do tomorrow and putting a time beside it.
